claims.text: Toughness retention in equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys is governed jointly by heterogeneous lattice-strain-induced dislocation activity and nanoscale twin boundaries.
Heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behavior, including multiple kinks, jogs, and bidirectional cross-slip.
Heterogeneous lattice strain promotes nanoscale twin formation.
Nanoscale twinning provides an additional deformation mode that helps preserve toughness.
Nanoscale twins and complex dislocation structures absorb deformation energy and delay crack initiation and propagation.
A post-processing heat treatment can reduce lattice-strain heterogeneity and suppress nanoscale twins without changing the overall FCC structure.
Slight compositional adjustment can reduce lattice-strain heterogeneity and suppress nanoscale twins while retaining the FCC structure.
Reducing lattice-strain heterogeneity diminishes nanoscale twin density and alters dislocation behavior.
Reduced nanoscale twin density and altered dislocation behavior lower the capacity for plastic deformation and cause toughness loss.
The initial material is a homogeneous, equiatomic, single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
The initial material inherently contains heterogeneous lattice strain.
The initial material contains a natural population of nanoscale twins at room temperature.
Heat-treated samples will have lower fracture resistance or strain-to-failure than untreated samples.
The proposed behavior should hold under quasi-static loading from room temperature to approximately 800 degrees Celsius, provided the alloy remains FCC.
Single-phase FCC high- and medium-entropy alloys can rapidly lose ductility between 400 and 800 degrees Celsius.
The mechanism is expected to generalize to equiatomic or near-equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloys.
The mechanism's validity in non-FCC alloys and under very high strain-rate loading is uncertain.
The quantitative relationship among lattice-strain heterogeneity, nanoscale twin density, and toughness may vary with processing history and minor compositional fluctuations.
EBSD can identify nanoscale twins through their characteristic approximately 60-degree misorientation.
If strain heterogeneity and twin density are successfully reduced without a corresponding toughness reduction, the proposed governing mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis broadly expects the mechanism to hold up to approximately 800 degrees Celsius, while the cited conditions evidence reports rapid ductility loss in single-phase FCC HEAs/MEAs between 400 and 800 degrees Celsius. This does not strictly disprove the mechanism, but it makes the stated high-temperature boundary insufficiently qualified.

The intervention is only intended to suppress strain heterogeneity and nanoscale twins, yet the falsification rule treats failure of the treatment to produce those microstructural changes as falsification. A failed manipulation would not by itself contradict the proposed toughness mechanism.
